Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure, alerting you to potential high blood pressure, but will not provide an actual blood pressure reading.

Some smart rings and other fitness devices can also do this, but they require periodic calibration with a traditional cuff-style blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to be able to provide full blood pressure measurements without any calibration, and says trials involving thousands of people support this claim…

"Silent killer"

Both abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and abnormally low blood pressure (hypotension) can carry serious health risks.

Of the two, high blood pressure is the more dangerous, known as the "silent killer," because it can cause serious and irreversible damage to the arteries, heart, and brain without any obvious symptoms. This condition is often only discovered when it triggers a heart attack or stroke.

Especially for older people, it is best to monitor blood pressure regularly. Home cuff-style blood pressure monitors are available on the market for convenient self-measurement. However, if it could be monitored fully automatically through a fitness device worn daily, that would undoubtedly be more ideal.

Apple Watch blood pressure feature

The launch of watchOS 26 allows five Apple Watch models to measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these models will not provide any readings — they will only alert you when signs of possible high blood pressure are detected. Other devices such as the Oura Ring work in a similar way.

Some fitness devices on the market can provide actual blood pressure readings, but they require periodic calibration using measurements from a cuff-style blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup Vital Signals says its smart ring, called the Signal Ring, can achieve accuracy on par with traditional upper-arm cuff blood pressure monitors without any calibration required.

Bloomberg reports that the company's CEO, Tom Moss, revealed that he himself nearly died because his high blood pressure went undiagnosed, which prompted him to found the company.

Signal Ring goes on pre-order later today, ships in October, is priced at US$399, and requires no subscription. The companion app displays blood pressure readings in real time as well as long-term blood pressure trends (as shown in the image above).

It is worth noting that the Oura Ring has not yet received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but clinical trials have shown that the ring can provide accurate blood pressure readings across thousands of participants.

Interestingly, Moss has no intention of marketing the Signal Ring to all consumers. He says features of this kind are best suited to older people, and to groups assessed by doctors as being at risk of high blood pressure; the implication being that the Signal Ring may not stand out in other areas (such as sleep tracking).
